Production UI Architecture & Composition
Define responsibilities for layouts, pages, features and interactive islands

Phase 20 - Production Application UI
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend

Architecture milestone

Route

Protected layout

Phase 20 turns the secure full-stack foundation into a coherent, accessible application interface without moving business authority into the
browser.

A production UI is an architecture, not a collection of cards
A polished interface starts with responsibility boundaries. The page owns route-level composition. The shell owns
persistent navigation and workspace context. Feature components own domain presentation. Small client islands own
local interaction. The API remains the source of truth for server state and authorization.

Layer                                  Responsibility

Root layout                            Fonts, global styles, top-level metadata

Protected (app) layout                 Session gate + application shell

Page                                   Route-specific data and composition

Feature component                      Task/project/workspace presentation

Client island                          Menu toggle, disclosure, local interaction

NestJS API                             Authoritative data, rules, authorization

Figure 1 - UI composition

Route request

v

Protected layout verifies session

v

Page fetches authorized API data

v

Server Components render structure

v

Client islands hydrate where needed

v

Browser interaction

The client bundle stays smaller when static/data-rendering components remain on the server.

Do not make the whole shell a Client Component

Next.js pages and layouts are Server Components by default. Add `use client` only at the boundary that actually needs state,
event handlers, effects, or browser APIs.

What not to optimize yet
• No design-system package just to get a button component.

• No global state store for navigation that URL/layout state already solves.

• No client-side fetching library yet - TanStack Query is Phase 22.

• No drag-and-drop board yet - responsive, keyboard-friendly CRUD surfaces come first.

Protected Route Groups & App Layout
Organize authenticated application routes without changing public URLs

Phase 20 - Production Application UI
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend

Architecture milestone

(app) route group

v

Session verification

v

AppShell

v

Route content

Phase 20 turns the secure full-stack foundation into a coherent, accessible application interface without moving business authority into the
browser.

Route groups let us organize without changing URLs
The App Router can group authenticated application routes under `(app)` while keeping clean URLs such as `/tasks`
and `/projects`. The protected layout becomes the natural place to verify the Supabase session and render the shared
shell.

src/app/
■■■ layout.tsx
■■■ signin/
■■■ auth/
■■■ (app)/
■■■ layout.tsx
■■■ dashboard/page.tsx
■■■ projects/page.tsx
■■■ tasks/
■    ■■■ page.tsx
■    ■■■ loading.tsx
■    ■■■ error.tsx
■    ■■■ not-found.tsx
■■■ account/page.tsx

Protected layout
export default async function AppLayout({ children }) {
const supabase = await createClient()
const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.getClaims()

if (error || !data?.claims?.sub) redirect('/signin')

return <AppShell user={...}>{children}</AppShell>
}

Route protection here improves UX, but API authorization still wins

A user could call NestJS without rendering this layout. Phase 18/19 guards and authorization remain mandatory.

Shared layout should remain stable
The shell should survive navigation so users keep orientation. Route content changes inside `` while navigation and
account context stay visually consistent.

Phase 20 turns the secure full-stack foundation into a coherent, accessible application interface without moving business authority into the
browser.

Application shell: persistent orientation
The shell has three jobs: primary navigation, current workspace/account context, and a predictable place for route
content. It should not become a giant stateful component that owns every feature.

Figure 1 - Shell layout

Sidebar / mobile navigation

v

Header / workspace + account

v

Main content region

v

Route page

Persistent navigation surrounds changing route content.

Semantic landmarks
• `` for the desktop sidebar where appropriate.

• `` for route links.

• `` for account/workspace context.

• `` for route content.

• Skip link for keyboard users to bypass repeated navigation.

Navigation target size
TaskFlow gives primary navigation and buttons at least a comfortable 44px interaction height, exceeding WCAG 2.2
minimum target-size requirements and improving touch usability.

Shell decision                                  Reason

Sticky desktop sidebar                          Navigation stays available during long pages

Contained main width                            Very wide screens do not produce unreadably stretched content

Responsive collapse                             Mobile does not inherit a 260px permanent sidebar

Text labels                                     Icons alone are ambiguous and harder to learn

Visible focus                                   Keyboard users can track position

Sticky UI can hide focus

WCAG 2.2 adds Focus Not Obscured. Test keyboard navigation around sticky headers/footers so the focused element remains
visible.

Task Table & Domain Presentation Present operational data with semantic, responsive and scannable UI Phase 20 - Production Application UI Volume 06 - Professional Frontend Architecture milestone Authorized task data v Semantic table v Status/priority/assignee v Responsive table region Phase 20 turns the secure full-stack foundation into a coherent, accessible application interface without moving business authority into the browser. A data table should be a table when the data is tabular Tasks are naturally compared across columns: status, priority, assignee, due date. A semantic HTML table provides relationships that div-based card grids must recreate manually for assistive technology. ...
Tasks visible in your current workspace scope
Task Status Priority Assignee Due
Responsive strategy for real tables Do not collapse important business data into unreadable 320px cells. Keep a minimum table width and place it inside a labeled horizontal-scroll region. For mobile-first task workflows, a later alternate card/list view can be added intentionally rather than by CSS accident. Figure 1 - Table responsiveness Desktop: full table visible v Tablet: compressed but readable v Mobile: contained horizontal scroll v Future: optional purpose-built list view Horizontal scroll is acceptable when the content is genuinely tabular and the region is discoverable and keyboard reachable. Status and priority communicate with text + color A green pill labeled “Done” is better than a green dot with no accessible text. Color reinforces meaning but never carries it alone. Do not turn every row into one giant click target Keep the task title as a clear link and keep future row actions as real buttons. This preserves keyboard semantics and avoids nested interactive controls.

Visual System, CSS Modules & Design
Tokens
Build consistent styling without premature design-system dependencies

Phase 20 - Production Application UI
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend

Architecture milestone

Global tokens

v

CSS Modules

v

Reusable visual patterns

Phase 20 turns the secure full-stack foundation into a coherent, accessible application interface without moving business authority into the
browser.

A small visual system prevents random CSS
Phase 20 introduces design tokens through CSS custom properties: surfaces, text, borders, brand colors, spacing,
radii, and shadows. The goal is consistency, not creating a full design-system package before we need one.

:root {
--surface-canvas: #f5f7fb;
--surface-panel: #ffffff;
--text-primary: #172033;
--text-secondary: #627086;
--border-subtle: #dbe2ea;
--brand: #166b72;
--radius-md: 12px;
--space-4: 16px;
--space-6: 24px;
}

Global CSS vs CSS Modules
• Global CSS: reset, root variables, document-level body styles, shared focus behavior.

• CSS Modules: shell, table, badges, page header, empty state, feature components.

• Avoid global feature selectors that accidentally leak styles between routes.

Token group                   Examples                               Purpose

Surface                       canvas, panel, muted                   Layer hierarchy

Text                          primary, secondary                     Reading hierarchy

Semantic                      danger, warning, success               Meaning, always paired with text/icons

Space                         4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32                   Consistent rhythm

Radius                        sm, md, lg                             Consistent component shape

Do not chase visual uniqueness at the cost of usability

A production business UI should feel predictable. Consistency, readable density, and clear hierarchy matter more than
decorative novelty.

Loading, Empty, Error & Not-Found States
Design explicit states for every route outcome

Phase 20 - Production Application UI
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend

Architecture milestone

Request begins

v

Loading

v

Success/empty/error/not-found

v

Recovery

Phase 20 turns the secure full-stack foundation into a coherent, accessible application interface without moving business authority into the
browser.

A production page has more than a success state
Every route that depends on network/data conditions needs deliberate loading, empty, error, unauthorized, forbidden,
and not-found experiences. “Nothing rendered” is not an acceptable state.

State                                What the UI should communicate

Loading                              Work is in progress; preserve surrounding shell

Empty                                Request succeeded; no matching data

Error                                Request failed; recovery action if possible

Not found                            Resource unavailable / inaccessible

Unauthorized                         Authentication required; usually redirect/sign-in

Forbidden                            Caller is authenticated but cannot perform action

Next.js route state files
tasks/
■■■ page.tsx
■■■ loading.tsx
■■■ error.tsx          // Client Component; gets reset()
■■■ not-found.tsx

Error boundary behavior
Next.js `error.tsx` wraps a route segment in an error boundary and must be a Client Component. Its `reset()` callback
can retry rendering the segment, making it appropriate for recoverable route failures.

Empty is not error

A 200 response with zero matching tasks is a successful state. Give users context and a next step, such as clearing filters or
creating a task.

Skeletons later, semantics now
Phase 20 may use simple text/loading placeholders. Skeleton polish can be added when it mirrors the final layout.
Avoid fake progress indicators that provide no information.

Accessibility, Keyboard & Focus
Architecture
Build WCAG 2.2 thinking into component behavior and semantics

Phase 20 - Production Application UI
Volume 06 - Professional Frontend

Architecture milestone

Semantic structure

Phase 20 turns the secure full-stack foundation into a coherent, accessible application interface without moving business authority into the
browser.

Accessibility is component architecture
TaskFlow targets WCAG 2.2 AA thinking from the beginning. The goal is not a “compliance page” at the end; keyboard
behavior, focus, labels, semantics, target size, reflow, and error communication influence how components are
designed.

Concern                             TaskFlow pattern

Keyboard                            Every action is a link/button/form control, not clickable divs

Focus                               Visible `:focus-visible`; no sticky UI fully hides focus

Bypass                              Skip link to `#main-content`

Target size                         Primary controls designed around >=44px comfort; never crowd tiny targets

State                               Status uses text + color

Tables                              caption, th, scope, labeled scroll region

Zoom/reflow                         Test at narrow widths and 200% zoom

Why 24px and 44px both appear in accessibility discussions
WCAG 2.2 AA introduces a 24x24 CSS pixel minimum target-size criterion with exceptions. A 44x44 target is the
stronger enhanced target and remains a practical design goal for primary controls, especially touch interfaces.

functions, database clients, or secrets into a client island.

lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 20: Production Application UI

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
route/layout -> server data boundary -> page composition -> client interaction islands -> responsive/accessibility states

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Only styling the success state
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Global client component wrapping the whole app
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Clickable divs without keyboard semantics

Failure drill 4 — Mobile layout treated as desktop squeezed smaller

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Production Application UI

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 20 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Build a production application shell and reusable UI states instead of isolated demo components.

Required artifact
TaskFlow responsive shell with navigation, workspace context, task screens, loading/empty/error states, and accessible interactions.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can compose a shell from reusable patterns.
• Can model all UI states.
• Can choose server/client boundaries.
• Can verify basic accessibility and responsive behavior.

Independent build sequence
1. Design the application shell first: sidebar/topbar/main content/mobile navigation.
2. Create reusable primitives for page header, panel/card, empty state, loading skeleton, and error state.
3. Build workspace/board/task navigation with active state derived from routing rather than duplicated local state.
4. Compose Server and Client Components so interactive islands remain small.
5. Test keyboard focus, labels, landmarks, reduced-motion expectations, and narrow widths.
6. Exercise all non-happy states by forcing no data, slow data, error, and forbidden responses.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 20: Production Application UI. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
TaskFlow responsive shell with navigation, workspace context, task screens, loading/empty/error states, and accessible interactions.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

# Phase 20 accessibility checklist

- Semantic landmarks: header, nav, main, aside where appropriate.
- One meaningful page h1.
- Skip link reaches main content.
- All interactive controls work by keyboard.
- Focus indicator remains visible and not obscured.
- Target size aims for at least 44px for primary controls and never relies on tiny adjacent click targets.

The production UI uses the App Router with a protected `(app)` route group.

Server Components own:
- authenticated layout checks,
- initial page data fetching,
- metadata and route composition,
- permission-derived server rendering.

Client Components are kept as islands for:
- mobile menu toggle,
- local disclosure controls,
- browser-only interactions.

The UI does not become the security boundary. Hidden controls improve experience, but NestJS Phase 19 authorization remains authoritative.
